headline: H.R. 973 itself has only a 25.7% chance of becoming the law, but there is a 66.6% chance that a mandatory UL battery standard reaches VoltRide anyway, and doing nothing would cost an expected $3.77 million in the first year, so the company should certify Shenzhen PowerCell and the VoltRide Cargo e-bike now rather than wait.
bill_in_plain_english: The bill tells the Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC), the federal agency that writes safety rules for consumer products, to turn three existing voluntary safety standards for lithium-ion batteries and the e-bikes and e-scooters that use them into mandatory federal rules within 180 days of the bill becoming law. After that, manufacturers and sellers of these products would have to meet the UL 2271, UL 2849 and UL 2272 standards, and future revisions to those standards would become mandatory automatically unless the agency objects. The bill passed the House on 2025-04-28 by 365 votes to 42 and is now in the Senate.

odds.probability_text: 25.7% chance of becoming law this Congress
why: The bill has a matching bill in the Senate (S. 389), which multiplies its odds by 2.02.
It has cosponsors from both parties, which multiplies its odds by 1.52.

Only 71 days are left in this Congress. If it does not pass both chambers by 2027-01-03, it dies and must be reintroduced. Having many cosponsors slightly lowers the odds (a 0.91 multiplier), while the broad coalition of industry, consumer and fire-service groups backing a mandatory UL standard raised them (a 1.2 multiplier).
what_would_change_it: A final CPSC rule would deliver most of the bill's substance without the bill, which may make the Senate feel less urgency even as it confirms the policy is coming.
The Senate companion S. 389 was reported by the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee on 2025-07-29 and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar (Calendar No. 133), where it has stayed.
The CPSC proposed its own mandatory micromobility battery standard on 2026-06-24, closed written comments on 2026-08-24 and held an oral-comment hearing on 2026-10-21; a final rule is pending.
The CPSC regained a three-member quorum in early August 2026, which lets it resume rulemakings.
Litigation over a CPSC final rule could delay or cancel it, which would revive the case for the bill.

what_it_means: The single most likely outcome is not the bill but a CPSC rule: there is a 40.9% chance the agency finalizes its own broader micromobility battery rule in about 12 months, and a 33.4% chance the bill dies and nothing changes.

If VoltRide does nothing, the expected first-year impact is -$3.77 million and the worst case is -$5.68 million. VoltRide City, VoltRide Cargo and the Replacement battery pack would all become unsellable once a rule applies, and gross margin after the rule falls to 0.0%.

The best option, certifying Shenzhen PowerCell and the VoltRide Cargo e-bike, has an expected first-year impact of -$226 thousand and a worst case of -$266 thousand, and it is compliant in every scenario where the bill passes. Certifying costs $60 thousand in every scenario, plus $35 thousand of re-testing if the CPSC rule is the route; it carries no unsellable-stock charge.

Switching suppliers also makes current stock unsellable: $574 thousand if VoltRide moves all battery volume to Hanbit Energy and Dongguan SafeCell, and $406.6 thousand if it waits and reacts. That is why those two options have expected first-year impacts of -$915 thousand and -$644 thousand.

VoltRide has about 8 months (probability 9.0%) in the fastest pass scenario. Certifying the VoltRide Cargo electrical system takes 16 weeks and getting Shenzhen PowerCell to UL 2271 takes about 26 weeks, so a slow start means lost sales; the 2,800 packs already in inventory were built to EN 15194 only and must be sold or written down before a rule applies.

recommendation.summary: Prepare now: pay to bring Shenzhen PowerCell packs to UL 2271 (about 26 weeks, roughly 15% higher pack price) and certify the VoltRide Cargo electrical system to UL 2849 ($60 thousand, 16 weeks).
recommendation.why: It has both the best expected first-year impact of any option at -$226 thousand and the best worst case at -$266 thousand, and it is compliant in every scenario where the bill passes. It also keeps the 5,000-unit contract minimum with Shenzhen PowerCell and avoids the $75 thousand early-exit penalty that both switching options pay. Certifying costs $60 thousand in every scenario, plus $35 thousand of re-testing if the CPSC rule is the route, and carries no unsellable-stock charge.
recommendation.tradeoff: It beats the next-best option, wait and react (expected -$644 thousand), on both expected impact and worst case, so its real cost shows up in the one scenario where it loses: the scenario where the bill dies and nothing changes. There certifying costs $266,325 in the first year while wait and react costs nothing. That $266,325 is what VoltRide pays for being ready, and with a 66.6% chance that a mandatory standard arrives from either the bill or the CPSC's own rule, that is a price worth paying.
switch_if: Shenzhen PowerCell's roughly 26-week certification timeline slips past the point where packs would be ready for the 8-month fastest compliance date, which would make moving volume to Hanbit Energy and Dongguan SafeCell the safer path even though it now carries $574 thousand of unsellable stock.
Shenzhen PowerCell cannot hold its price increase near 15%, or asks for a much larger increase than the analysis assumes.
The CPSC final rule is vacated in court or formally withdrawn, which moves VoltRide toward the case where the bill dies and nothing changes, where doing nothing costs 0 and certifying costs $266,325.
The Senate does not take up S. 389 before the 71 days run out and the CPSC docket stalls, raising the odds of no rule at all.

options_compared.name: Prepare now: certify Shenzhen PowerCell and the VoltRide Cargo e-bike
options_compared.one_line: Best expected result and best worst case, compliant in every pass scenario; costs $60 thousand in every scenario plus $35 thousand of re-testing if the CPSC rule lands, with no unsellable-stock charge.

options_compared.name: Wait and react: move only when a rule is final
options_compared.one_line: Costs nothing if the bill dies and nothing changes, but in the compliance scenarios it pays $60 thousand for Cargo, a $75 thousand exit penalty and $406.6 thousand of unsellable stock.

options_compared.name: Prepare now: move battery volume to Hanbit Energy and Dongguan SafeCell
options_compared.one_line: Certified from day one, but every compliance scenario adds a $75 thousand exit penalty and $574 thousand of unsellable stock on top of the $60 thousand Cargo certification.

options_compared.name: Prepare now: drop Cargo, keep City and spare packs, certify Shenzhen PowerCell
options_compared.one_line: Compliant with no unsellable-stock charge and a 40.7% margin, but giving up the VoltRide Cargo line costs far more than certifying it.

options_compared.name: Do nothing
options_compared.one_line: Costs nothing only if the bill dies and nothing changes; otherwise VoltRide City, VoltRide Cargo and the Replacement battery pack become unsellable, margin falls to 0.0%, and a $50 thousand exit penalty applies in most compliance scenarios.

next_steps.step: Sign the UL 2849 certification contract for the VoltRide Cargo electrical system and start the 16-week testing work.

Put Shenzhen PowerCell on a written UL 2271 certification plan with dated milestones against its roughly 26-week estimate, and get the price increase and the 5,000-unit annual contract minimum confirmed in writing.
next_steps.by_when: Before the next purchase order, and no later than 2026-12-01

next_steps.step: Sell down or write down the 2,800 EN 15194-only packs in inventory before any compliance date, and stop reordering that version so stock does not grow into an unsellable-stock charge.
next_steps.by_when: Ongoing, reviewed monthly until the inventory is cleared

next_steps.step: Track the CPSC docket and the Senate calendar for S. 389 weekly, and escalate if the final rule slips, is litigated, or oral comments point to an effective date later than 180 days.
next_steps.by_when: Weekly from now; escalate immediately on any CPSC final rule or Senate floor action

next_steps.step: Budget the $60 thousand Cargo certification and about $25 thousand a year for tracking and re-testing against rolling UL revisions under the bill's auto-update clause.

opportunities: Competitor Zoomly's mostly uncertified low-cost line should lose share once certification is mandatory, giving VoltRide an estimated 3% unit volume lift in the City and Cargo lines.

Hanbit Energy (4,000 units a year) and Dongguan SafeCell (6,000 units a year) already meet the standards and together have enough capacity for all 9,000 packs VoltRide needs, so locking that capacity early is both a hedge and an advantage.
VoltRide City is already UL 2849 certified, so the company can market a fully certified City and Cargo lineup while rivals are still testing.

California SB 1271 sales and lease duties have applied since 2026-01-01 and New York City Local Law 39 since 2023, so national retailers and rental fleets already need certified suppliers and can be sold on VoltRide.
assumptions_to_verify: That CPSC's added post-discharge, reverse-polarity and labeling requirements force about $35 thousand of one-time re-testing and relabeling per product family (low confidence).
That Hanbit Energy and Dongguan SafeCell will pass through only about 8% in certification and testing cost (low confidence).
That Zoomly's uncertified line really loses share and gives VoltRide about a 3% unit volume lift (low confidence).
That the slow case of about 30 months after enactment, driven by OMB review, quorum problems or litigation, is realistic (low confidence).
